whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Tableau Architect exam for?

personas.label: Enterprise Architects
personas.description: Professionals designing large-scale Tableau deployments with multi-node server topology, high availability, and disaster recovery.

personas.label: Tableau Server Admins Moving Up
personas.description: Experienced administrators who want to validate their skills in architecture design, security planning, and governance frameworks.

personas.label: BI Platform Leads
personas.description: Leaders responsible for Tableau platform scalability, performance optimization, content management, and enterprise data governance.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Tableau Architect Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: The Tableau Architect exam is one of the harder Tableau certifications. It tests deep knowledge of Tableau Server topology, multi-node clustering, row-level security, and enterprise governance — surface-level familiarity with Tableau administration is not enough to pass.
bullets: 45 questions in 90 minutes — roughly two minutes per question, but architecture scenarios often require careful analysis.
~70% passing score — you need approximately 32 correct answers out of 45 to pass.
Enterprise-scale depth required — questions test server process distribution, HA configuration, RLS implementation patterns, and content governance at scale.
Hands-on architecture experience is critical — candidates who have designed or managed multi-node Tableau Server environments with security layers and governance frameworks are best prepared.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Book when you can confidently design a Tableau Server topology, configure row-level security, plan disaster recovery, and build a governance framework without referencing documentation.

examFormat.heading: Tableau Architect Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: The exam is proctored online or in-person. Here is the format:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Scenario questions describe enterprise environments and ask you to design the correct server topology, security model, or governance framework for the given requirements.
bestWayToPass: Server topology: Know every Tableau Server process (VizQL, Data Server, Backgrounder, Repository) and how to distribute them across nodes for performance and redundancy.
Security layers: Master site roles, content permissions, and row-level security implementation patterns including user filters and entitlement tables.
Performance tuning: Understand extract optimization, Backgrounder sizing, workbook performance analysis, and the Performance Recorder tool.
Governance design: Study project hierarchies, content certification, Data Catalog lineage, and content lifecycle management for enterprise environments.

certificationCard.description: Tableau Architects design and govern enterprise Tableau analytics solutions. They define architecture, governance, scalability, and best practices for Tableau Server and Tableau Cloud.

keyConcepts.h2: Tableau Architect: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Tableau Platform Architecture and Deployment
blocks.body: **Tableau Server** is the on-premise or customer-managed cloud deployment. Tableau Cloud is the fully managed SaaS offering. Server architecture: primary node runs all processes; worker nodes scale individual processes (VizQL Server, Data Server, Backgrounder, Application Server). Process distribution: VizQL renders visualisations; Backgrounder runs extract refreshes and subscriptions; Data Server manages data connections and caching. The architect selects the deployment model (Server vs Cloud) based on data residency, security, and operational capability requirements.

blocks.heading: Data Architecture: Published Data Sources and Extracts
blocks.body: Published Data Sources are centrally managed connections shared across workbooks — changes to the data source propagate to all workbooks using it. Embedded data sources are local to the workbook — simpler but harder to govern. Live connections query the database in real time; **extracts** (.hyper files) snapshot data for fast performance. **Tableau Prep** Builder creates ETL **pipelines** that output clean, reshaped data. The architect designs the data source strategy — which sources to publish, what extract schedules to run, and when live connections are appropriate.

blocks.heading: Security Architecture: Users, Groups, and Row-Level Security
blocks.body: **Tableau Server** security layers: Site Roles define what a user can do on the server. Content permissions control who can view, edit, or publish each workbook or data source. Row-Level Security (RLS) filters data based on the logged-in user — implemented via user filters in the data source, **calculated fields** using USERNAME() and ISMEMBEROF(), or entitlement tables joined to the data. The architect designs the RLS implementation based on the complexity of the access model (single-attribute vs multi-attribute vs role-based entitlement table).

blocks.heading: Performance Optimisation and Scalability
blocks.body: Workbook performance factors: number of marks in the view, query complexity, extract size, and use of context filters. Performance Recorder in **Tableau Desktop** identifies slow queries and rendering. Extract optimisation: aggregating **extracts**, filtering to only needed rows, hiding unused fields. Server-level: worker node sizing for Backgrounder (concurrent extract refreshes) and VizQL (concurrent view renders). Tableau Workbook Advisor (Tableau Cloud) flags performance anti-patterns. The architect balances user experience performance with infrastructure cost.

blocks.heading: Governance and Content Management at Scale
blocks.body: Projects organise content with inherited permissions — nested projects allow hierarchical governance. Content certification marks high-quality, approved data sources and workbooks. Data Catalog (Tableau Catalog — part of Data Management Add-on) provides data lineage, field-level metadata, quality warnings, and impact analysis. Usage analytics in the Admin area show which workbooks are accessed and which are stale (candidates for archival). The architect designs the governance framework — project hierarchy, certification process, naming conventions, and content lifecycle management.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Tableau Architect Exam
scenarioTips.intro: The Tableau Architect exam tests enterprise-scale Tableau deployment design. Focus on server architecture, performance optimization, security configuration, and designing scalable self-service analytics environments.

blocks.heading: Tableau Server Architecture
blocks.body: Know the **Tableau Server** component topology: Gateway, Application Server, VizQL Server, Data Server, Backgrounder, and Repository. Understand how each component scales and where bottlenecks occur in high-usage environments.

blocks.heading: Performance Optimization
blocks.body: Know how to optimize extract refreshes (incremental vs. full), optimize workbook performance (data source optimization, context filters, reducing marks), and configure Backgrounder for large extract loads.

blocks.heading: Security Architecture
blocks.body: Understand Tableau's multi-layer security: server-level (authentication), site-level (content permissions), data-level (row-level security via user filters or VPD). Know how to implement data-level security at scale.

blocks.heading: High Availability & Disaster Recovery
blocks.body: Know how to configure **Tableau Server** for HA: multi-node cluster, repository failover (PostgreSQL clustering), and backup strategies. Understand TSM backup/restore and the Tableau Cloud migration options.

blocks.heading: Governance Framework
blocks.body: Know how to design a data governance framework in Tableau: certified data sources, data quality warnings, column-level descriptions, and Tableau Catalog for data lineage and impact analysis.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Tableau Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: After this Tableau certification, consider other Tableau credentials or CRM Analytics:

sampleQuestions.question: What is the primary focus of a Salesforce Certified Tableau Architect?
options: Designing and governing enterprise Tableau analytics solutions at scale
sampleQuestions.explanation: Tableau Architects design and govern enterprise Tableau analytics solutions, including architecture, governance, and scalability.
whyWrong: Creating individual dashboards is a narrower analyst task, not the enterprise-scale governance focus of an architect.
Managing Salesforce CRM data is unrelated to Tableau's own architecture and governance concerns.
Marketing automation is unrelated to Tableau architecture.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Tableau deployment consideration is critical for an architect?
options: Server topology, scalability, high availability, and security
sampleQuestions.explanation: Architects must consider server topology, scalability, high availability, and security for enterprise Tableau deployments.
whyWrong: Color schemes are a design detail, not a deployment-scale architectural consideration.
Dashboard count alone doesn't capture the full scalability/HA/security considerations an architect must address.
User count alone doesn't capture the full topology/scalability/security considerations of deployment architecture.

sampleQuestions.question: What role does Tableau's VizQL engine play in architecture decisions?
options: Translates drag-and-drop actions into database queries and optimizes performance
sampleQuestions.explanation: VizQL translates visual design into database queries. Architects must understand its impact on data source design and query performance.
whyWrong: VizQL doesn't just render static images — it dynamically generates optimized queries from user interactions.
VizQL isn't the authentication mechanism — that's a separate concern (SSO/SAML).
VizQL isn't a licensing management tool — that's unrelated to its query-generation role.

sampleQuestions.question: Which authentication method supports single sign-on (SSO) for Tableau Server?
options: SAML 2.0, Kerberos, OpenID Connect, and trusted ticketing
sampleQuestions.explanation: Tableau Server supports SAML 2.0, Kerberos, OpenID Connect, and trusted ticketing for SSO and enterprise identity integration.
whyWrong: Local authentication alone doesn't provide the SSO capability the question asks about.
LDAP alone is a directory protocol, not itself an SSO mechanism the way SAML/Kerberos/OIDC are.
OAuth 1.0 is an older, less common protocol — modern Tableau SSO relies on SAML 2.0, Kerberos, and OpenID Connect.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of Tableau's repository database?
options: Stores metadata, user info, permissions, and extract info for Tableau Server
sampleQuestions.explanation: The repository stores metadata, permissions, schedules, and extract information. Architects plan for its backup and scalability.
whyWrong: 'Stores user data' alone undersells the repository's broader role, which includes metadata, permissions, and extract info.
'Stores only workbooks' undersells the repository's broader scope beyond just workbook files.
'Manages extracts only' undersells the repository's broader role beyond just extract metadata.

sampleQuestions.question: Which factor affects Tableau Server scalability the most?
options: Concurrent user load, background job load, and data source performance
sampleQuestions.explanation: Scalability depends on concurrent users, background jobs (extracts, subscriptions), and underlying data source performance.
whyWrong: Dashboard color themes are a visual design detail, not a scalability factor.
Number of workbooks alone doesn't capture the concurrent-load and performance factors that most affect scalability.
Font sizes are a visual design detail, unrelated to server scalability.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a Tableau data server used for?
options: Centralizing published data sources for reuse and governance across workbooks
sampleQuestions.explanation: Data servers let you publish and reuse data sources across workbooks, improving consistency and governance.
whyWrong: Serving generic web content isn't the data server's specific purpose — that's about centralizing published data sources.
Hosting Tableau Server itself is a different infrastructure concern, not what a data server specifically provides.
Managing licenses is unrelated to the data server's data-source centralization purpose.

sampleQuestions.question: Which governance practice helps control Tableau content proliferation?
options: Promoting certified data sources, using projects for organization, and setting ownership policies
sampleQuestions.explanation: Certified data sources, project structure, and ownership policies help govern content at scale.
whyWrong: Disabling all sharing would hurt collaboration, the opposite of a sound content-governance practice.
Removing all extracts would hurt performance, not help control content proliferation.
Limiting users to one workbook is an impractical, overly restrictive approach, not the actual recommended governance practice.

sampleQuestions.question: What does Tableau's backgrounder process handle?
options: Extract refreshes, subscriptions, and other scheduled jobs
sampleQuestions.explanation: The backgrounder process runs extract refreshes, subscriptions, and other scheduled tasks. Architects size it for job load.
whyWrong: User sessions are a different concern, not what the backgrounder process specifically handles.
VizQL rendering happens in real-time during interaction, not as a background scheduled job.
License validation is a separate administrative function, not what the backgrounder specifically handles.

sampleQuestions.question: Which high-availability configuration uses multiple Tableau Server nodes?
options: Distributed deployment with multiple application servers and a gateway
sampleQuestions.explanation: Distributed deployment spreads services across nodes for high availability and load distribution.
whyWrong: A single-node deployment is the opposite of the multi-node HA configuration being described.
A development server is a non-production environment, not the HA configuration being asked about.
Cloud-only deployment describes Tableau Cloud, not the on-premises multi-node HA configuration being described.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the benefit of Tableau extracts (.tde/.hyper) for performance?
options: They pre-aggregate and compress data, reducing load on source systems and improving query speed
sampleQuestions.explanation: Extracts pre-aggregate and compress data, offloading work from source systems and speeding up queries.
whyWrong: Extracts don't reduce the number of colors — that's unrelated to their performance purpose.
Extracts don't only store images — they store optimized, compressed data for query performance.
Extracts aren't a licensing management tool — that's unrelated to their performance purpose.

sampleQuestions.question: Which security layer controls who can view or edit Tableau content?
options: Project permissions, workbook permissions, and row-level security
sampleQuestions.explanation: Project and workbook permissions plus row-level security control access to Tableau content.
whyWrong: Data source permissions alone don't cover the full security layering (project, workbook, row-level) the question describes.
VizQL alone is the query engine, not itself a security/access-control layer.
The repository alone stores metadata — it isn't itself the permission-enforcement layer for content viewing.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a best practice for Tableau Server disaster recovery?
options: Regular repository backups, documented restore procedures, and testing recovery
sampleQuestions.explanation: Regular repository backups and tested restore procedures are essential for disaster recovery.
whyWrong: 'No backups needed' contradicts the fundamental disaster-recovery best practice of regular backups.
Backing up only workbooks misses the repository data essential for full recovery.
'Single-node only' contradicts the resilience goal disaster recovery planning is meant to achieve.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Tableau Cloud consideration differs from on-premises Server?
options: Managed infrastructure, built-in high availability, and connectivity to cloud data sources
sampleQuestions.explanation: Tableau Cloud is fully managed with built-in HA; architects focus on connectivity and data source design.
whyWrong: 'No difference' contradicts the real, documented differences between Tableau Cloud and Server.
'No authentication' contradicts the fact that Tableau Cloud has its own authentication considerations.
'No governance' contradicts the fact that governance still applies differently in a cloud-managed context.

sampleQuestions.question: What does incremental refresh do for Tableau extracts?
options: Refreshes only new or changed rows based on a key, reducing refresh time
sampleQuestions.explanation: Incremental refresh updates only new or changed rows, improving refresh performance for large datasets.
whyWrong: Refreshing all data every time is the opposite of what incremental refresh is designed to avoid.
Incremental refresh doesn't delete old data — it adds/updates based on a key.
Incremental refresh doesn't change colors — that's unrelated to its data-refresh function.
